additive-manufacturing-001.question: In the ISO/ASTM 52900 classification, which category of additive manufacturing applies to a process that extrudes a thermoplastic filament through a heated nozzle and builds up a shape one layer at a time, as if drawing lines?
choices: Material extrusion
Binder jetting
Vat photopolymerization
additive-manufacturing-001.explanation: ISO/ASTM 52900 divides additive manufacturing into seven categories according to the principle by which the material is consolidated. A process that pushes molten material out of a nozzle and lays it down is material extrusion, of which FFF (fused filament fabrication) with polymer filament is the typical example. Binder jetting sprays a binder by inkjet onto a spread layer of powder to glue the particles together, without melting the material itself. Vat photopolymerization cures a liquid photopolymer resin filling a vat with ultraviolet or other light. The other categories are powder bed fusion, which melts powder with heat; directed energy deposition, which melts fed material on the spot; material jetting, which deposits droplets of material; and sheet lamination, which bonds sheets together.

additive-manufacturing-002.question: Laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) is carried out with a laser power P = 200 W, scan speed v = 800 mm/s, hatch spacing h = 0.10 mm and layer thickness t = 0.030 mm. Which is closest to the volumetric energy density E = P/(v·h·t)?
choices: About 8.3 J/mm³
About 83 J/mm³
About 2.5 J/mm³
additive-manufacturing-002.explanation: E = P/(v·h·t) = 200/(800 × 0.10 × 0.030) = 200/2.4 ≈ 83 J/mm³. The denominator v·h·t is the volume of layer melted per second (mm³/s), so E is a guide to the energy delivered to a unit volume of powder. About 8.3 J/mm³ is the value obtained by forgetting to multiply by the hatch spacing, and about 2.5 J/mm³ by forgetting the layer thickness; both are really quantities in J/mm². If E is too small, lack of fusion occurs, and if it is too large, keyhole porosity appears more readily. However, even at the same E, the melt-pool shape changes with the combination of power and speed, so E is only a guide for comparing conditions on a common basis.

additive-manufacturing-003.question: In L-PBF, which type of pore is most likely to be found in a part built with the power set high and the scan speed too slow?
choices: Irregular pores spreading along the layer interfaces, with unmelted powder particles left inside
Uniform fine pores left where the spaces between powder particles shrank as in sintering
Nearly spherical pores near the bottom of the melt pool, formed when a deep vapor depression collapses
additive-manufacturing-003.explanation: When too much energy is delivered, the metal evaporates violently and the recoil pressure carves a narrow, deep vapor depression (a keyhole) into the melt pool. The keyhole is unstable, and when it collapses it traps gas near its bottom, leaving nearly spherical pores (keyhole porosity). Irregular pores along the layer interfaces with unmelted powder visible inside are, on the contrary, lack of fusion, which occurs when the energy is insufficient and the melt pool does not overlap enough with the neighboring scan tracks or the layer below. Uniform shrinkage of the spaces between particles as in sintering describes pores in a sintered body formed without melting, and is not the main origin of pores in L-PBF, which melts and solidifies the material. The proper conditions lie between the regions where these two types of pore appear.

additive-manufacturing-004.question: You want to repair a worn, chipped metal component, such as the tip of a gas-turbine blade, by building up material on only that part. Which combination of additive manufacturing process and reason is correct?
choices: Directed energy deposition, because powder or wire fed from a nozzle is melted on the spot and can be built up directly on an existing part
Powder bed fusion, because although it can only build inside a box of spread powder, its high precision can reproduce the repair shape in fine detail
Binder jetting, because powder is glued without melting, so there is no heat effect and the repair has the same strength as the base metal as built
additive-manufacturing-004.explanation: Directed energy deposition (DED) forms a melt pool with a laser, electron beam or arc and builds up material by feeding powder or wire into it from a nozzle. Because no powder bed is needed, material can be added directly onto the surface of an existing part, and DED is used to repair blades and dies, to build large parts and to make graded materials whose composition changes partway through. Because the melt pool is large and each layer thick, its shape accuracy and surface finish are inferior to those of powder bed fusion, and finish machining is assumed. Powder bed fusion can only build on a spread layer of powder and is not suited to adding material to a part of fixed shape. A binder-jetted part is a fragile body of particles that are merely glued together; it gains no strength until it is densified by sintering, which also shrinks it, so it cannot serve as a repair as built.

additive-manufacturing-005.question: Compared with L-PBF, which uses a laser, which is a correct feature of electron beam melting (EBM), the powder bed fusion process that melts metal powder with an electron beam?
choices: It can build in air and does not heat the powder bed, so parts can be removed right after building and residual stress is also small
It builds in vacuum while preheating the powder bed to a high temperature, so residual stress is small and in Ti-6Al-4V martensite is less likely to remain
Because an electron beam does not charge even insulators, ceramic or polymer powders can be melted and built in the same way as metal powders
additive-manufacturing-005.explanation: Electrons are scattered by gas molecules, so EBM is carried out in vacuum. To keep the beam from charging the powder and scattering it, the whole bed is preheated so that it is lightly sintered before melting, and for Ti-6Al-4V builds in which the part was held at around 700 °C have been reported. Because the temperature difference between the part and its surroundings is small, residual stress is small, and because the part is held hot, under ordinary conditions hardly any α′ martensite remains and an α + β microstructure forms. In exchange, the powder is coarser than for L-PBF (about 45–105 µm) and the layers are thicker, so the surface is rough and fine features are difficult. The option saying it builds in air without preheating contradicts the basics of EBM, vacuum and preheating. With an electron beam the charge must be conducted away, so non-conductive powders charge up and cannot be handled; in practice the process is limited to metals.

additive-manufacturing-006.question: In L-PBF, a single part 90 mm long, 20 mm wide and 20 mm thick is built. The layer thickness is 0.030 mm and spreading a new powder layer (recoating) takes 8.0 s per layer. Which is closest to the difference in total recoating time between standing the part with its long axis along the build direction and laying it down so that its height is 20 mm?
choices: About 1.5 hours
About 6.7 hours
About 5.2 hours
additive-manufacturing-006.explanation: The number of layers is the height divided by the layer thickness: 90/0.030 = 3000 layers standing and 20/0.030 ≈ 667 layers lying down. Recoating time is proportional to the number of layers, so the difference is (3000 − 667) × 8.0 s ≈ 1.87×10⁴ s ≈ 5.2 hours. About 6.7 hours is the total for the standing part (3000 × 8.0 s) and about 1.5 hours the total for the lying part; neither is the difference. In powder bed fusion, the time spent melting with the beam is set by the volume melted, but the recoating time is set by the height regardless of the number of parts. Placing parts low is therefore faster, and arranging many parts at the same height lowers the time per part. Orientation also changes the amount of support, residual stress and anisotropy from the layer direction, however, so it cannot be decided by time alone.

additive-manufacturing-007.question: In vat photopolymerization, assume that the cure depth Cd of the resin increases with the exposure E as Cd = Dp·ln(E/Ec) (the Jacobs equation). If the penetration depth of this resin is Dp = 0.12 mm and the critical exposure at which curing begins is Ec = 8.0 mJ/cm², which is closest to the exposure needed for a cure depth of 0.15 mm?
choices: About 10 mJ/cm²
About 28 mJ/cm²
About 142 mJ/cm²
additive-manufacturing-007.explanation: Solving the equation for E gives E = Ec·exp(Cd/Dp), so E = 8.0 × exp(0.15/0.12) = 8.0 × exp(1.25) ≈ 8.0 × 3.49 ≈ 28 mJ/cm². Light weakens exponentially in the resin and falls to 1/e at a depth Dp, so each time the exposure is multiplied by e (about 2.7), the cure depth increases by Dp. About 142 mJ/cm² is the value obtained by using the common logarithm instead of the natural logarithm, multiplying by 10^1.25, and about 10 mJ/cm² treats the relation as proportional without the logarithm, Ec × 1.25. In actual building, the cure depth is normally set somewhat larger than the layer thickness (overcure) to join the layers, and Dp and Ec are measured for each resin and machine.

additive-manufacturing-008.question: When an FCC Ni-base alloy or austenitic stainless steel is built by L-PBF, columnar grains extending across many layers along the build direction form, and a texture with 〈100〉 aligned with the build direction tends to develop. What is the main reason?
choices: Each new melt pool remelts part of the layer below, and the liquid solidifies on the remaining crystals, keeping their orientation
New crystals nucleate in the melt pool in every layer and then grow large by recrystallization during cooling, joining up with the layer below
The powder particles are originally single crystals oriented along 〈100〉, and the orientation of particles left unmelted is passed on directly to the part
additive-manufacturing-008.explanation: The melt pool melts a little into the layer below, so at the bottom of the melt pool the crystals of the lower layer are exposed directly as the solid–liquid interface. The liquid continues to solidify on those crystals with the same orientation (epitaxial growth), so grains extend across layers without new nucleation. Heat escapes mainly downward into the part, so the temperature gradient is close to the build direction, and in cubic crystals the grains whose 〈100〉 lies near that direction grow preferentially, producing a texture. If nucleation occurred in each layer, the result would be equiaxed grains about one layer thick, and the layers are not joined by recrystallization after solidification. The powder is normally polycrystalline, and its particles do not share a common orientation.

additive-manufacturing-009.question: The speed R at which the solid–liquid interface at the rear of the melt pool advances is given by R = v·cos θ, using the scan speed v and the angle θ between the interface normal (the solidification direction) and the scan direction. With v = 1.0 m/s, θ = 60° and a local temperature gradient of G = 2.0×10⁶ K/m, which is closest to the cooling rate G·R?
choices: About 2.0×10⁶ K/s
About 1.7×10⁶ K/s
About 1.0×10⁶ K/s
additive-manufacturing-009.explanation: The interface moves with the melt pool at v in the scan direction, so the speed at which it advances along its normal is R = v·cos θ = 1.0 × cos 60° = 0.50 m/s. The cooling rate is G·R = 2.0×10⁶ × 0.50 = 1.0×10⁶ K/s. About 2.0×10⁶ K/s is the value obtained by ignoring the angle and setting R = v, and about 1.7×10⁶ K/s by using sin instead of cos. At the bottom of the melt pool the interface is nearly horizontal, θ is close to 90° and R is close to 0, whereas near the surface at the rear end R approaches v. As a result, there is a tendency toward a planar interface or columnar grains at the bottom, where G/R is large, and toward equiaxed grains near the surface, where G/R is small, so the microstructure changes even within one melt pool.

additive-manufacturing-010.question: Ti-6Al-4V built by L-PBF often has high strength but low elongation in the as-built condition. Which is the correct as-built microstructure and reason?
choices: Fine acicular α′ martensite, because cooling from the melt pool is too fast for β to separate into α + β by diffusion
Coarse equiaxed α grains, because the layers below are reheated many times during building, fully recrystallize and grow large
Metastable β phase retained to room temperature, because rapid cooling stabilizes the β phase so that it stays BCC without transforming
additive-manufacturing-010.explanation: When Ti-6Al-4V is cooled quickly from the β temperature range, there is no time for it to separate into α and β by diffusion, and it transforms into α′ martensite by a diffusionless shear transformation. L-PBF cooling is very fast, so the microstructure consists of fine acicular α′ filling columnar prior-β grains elongated along the build direction, and the strength tends to be high but the elongation low. For this reason, heat treatment or HIP is used to decompose the α′ into α + β and restore ductility. This contrasts with EBM, where preheating keeps the part hot and a lamellar α + β microstructure readily forms during building. Coarse equiaxed grains from repeated heating is the opposite of what happens; the microstructure is fine and columnar. Retaining β to room temperature would require much more of β-stabilizing elements such as Mo and V, and in Ti-6Al-4V almost no β is retained even on quenching.

additive-manufacturing-011.question: In metal L-PBF, the part is often built attached to the base plate by supports, and after building it is given a stress-relief heat treatment while still on the plate before being cut off. Which is the correct reason for this procedure?
choices: The supports merely hold up overhanging regions from below, and the heat treatment sinters the powder stuck to the surface so that it is easier to remove
Rapid heating and cooling leave large residual stresses, so supports restrain warping and carry heat away, and the stress is lowered before removal to avoid distortion
The heat treatment rebonds the part–plate interface by diffusion so that the supports break off cleanly along that interface when the part is cut free
additive-manufacturing-011.explanation: A layer melted by the laser tries to contract as it solidifies and cools, but it is restrained by the cold layers beneath, so large residual stresses remain, tensile in the upper layers and compressive below. These stresses accumulate with every layer and can warp the part, peel it off the plate or crack it. The supports not only hold up overhanging regions but also anchor the part to the plate to restrain warping and conduct heat into the plate. If the part is cut off with the stresses still present, it distorts the moment the restraint is removed, so the stresses are first lowered by a stress-relief heat treatment and then the part is removed. Holding up overhangs is only part of what the supports do, and sintering surface powder is not the purpose of the heat treatment. Rebonding the interface would only make the part harder to remove, the opposite of the purpose.

additive-manufacturing-012.question: When tensile specimens of a metal built by L-PBF are pulled along the build direction (Z) and parallel to the layers (XY), the elongation in Z is often smaller and more scattered. Which is the correct main reason?
choices: In the Z direction the grains become fine and equiaxed, so the many grain boundaries hinder dislocation motion and work hardening saturates quickly
Z specimens take longer to build, so the upper layers are held hot longer and the whole specimen is annealed and softened
Flat lack-of-fusion defects spread between the layers are pulled open perpendicular to their plane under Z tension and readily act as crack origins
additive-manufacturing-012.explanation: Lack-of-fusion defects form where the melt pool did not fully overlap with the layer below or the neighboring scan track, so they are flat and spread along the plane of the layers. Pulled in XY, these flat defects are parallel to the load and hard to open, whereas in Z they are pulled perpendicular to their plane and open like sharp cracks. Z specimens therefore tend to fail early, with small and scattered elongation. Columnar grains elongated along the build direction and the texture also contribute to anisotropy. Fine equiaxed grains in the Z direction is the opposite of what happens; columnar grains grow along Z. If annealing from different times at high temperature were the main cause, the Z specimens would instead be softer and more ductile, which does not match the observations.

additive-manufacturing-013.question: A Ti-6Al-4V part made by powder bed fusion was given HIP, but when used with its as-built surface its fatigue strength hardly improved. Which is the correct reason?
choices: Gas enters surface-connected defects so they do not collapse, and the hollows of the rough surface remain as crack origins
The high temperature of HIP coarsens the α phase and greatly lowers the strength, cancelling the benefit of the reduced porosity
The high pressure of HIP creates new tensile residual stress at the surface, which hastens crack initiation from the surface
additive-manufacturing-013.explanation: HIP applies gas pressure from all directions at high temperature and collapses internal closed pores by creep and diffusion. Gas, the pressure medium, enters pores and lack-of-fusion defects connected to the surface, and the pressure inside and outside balances, so they do not collapse. In addition, the surface of a powder bed fusion part has a rough relief with half-melted powder attached, and HIP does not change its shape. Fatigue cracks start from such surface hollows and near-surface defects, so the benefit becomes clear when HIP is combined with machining the surface off to a sufficient depth. HIP may coarsen the microstructure a little and lower the strength slightly, but not enough to cancel the benefit of removing pores. An isotropic pressure is not, by itself, a treatment that creates tensile residual stress at the surface.

additive-manufacturing-014.question: High-strength aluminum alloys such as 7075 are prone to solidification cracking (hot cracking) when built by L-PBF as they are. Which method has been reported to prevent this cracking?
choices: Raising the laser power to increase the energy density, deepening the melt pool and slowing cooling, so that the columnar grains grow even longer
Adding Zr-containing fine particles to the powder as nuclei, so that fine equiaxed grains form instead of columnar ones and strain and liquid films are spread out
Increasing Zn and Mg to widen the freezing range further, so that the grain-boundary liquid films persist longer and absorb the shrinkage strain
additive-manufacturing-014.explanation: 7075 has a wide freezing range, and at the end of solidification thin liquid films persist at the grain boundaries for a long time. In L-PBF, long columnar grains grow in alignment, so the shrinkage strain during cooling concentrates on the liquid films at a few long grain boundaries, which are torn apart. In a method reported in 2017, Zr-containing nanoparticles were attached to the powder surface, forming Al₃Zr in the melt pool as sites for heterogeneous nucleation and giving fine equiaxed grains. The grain boundaries become numerous and short, so the strain is distributed and crack-free parts can be built. Raising the energy to lengthen the columnar grains only strengthens the crack-prone microstructure. Widening the freezing range so that the liquid films persist longer is counterproductive: the films cannot bear strain, so it only lengthens the time during which they are easily torn.

additive-manufacturing-015.question: A part whose shape was determined by topology optimization is to be made by metal additive manufacturing. Which correctly describes topology optimization and the points to consider when building?
choices: It is a method that changes given dimensions little by little to lower the stress; the number of holes and branches stays as in the initial shape, so any process can build it as is

It is a method that thickens the regions of high stress found by analysis; since the amount of material can be increased freely the part does not become lighter, but AM can always build it without supports
It keeps material only where needed to carry the loads within a given space, and build constraints such as overhang angles and powder-removal holes must also be included
additive-manufacturing-015.explanation: Topology optimization takes the space available for design and the load and restraint conditions, constrains the amount of material used, and computes where to place material so that an objective such as stiffness is optimized. Even the number of holes and branches (the topology) changes, often giving bone-like organic shapes that are hard to machine or cast, so it is considered a good match for additive manufacturing. However, even in powder bed fusion, near-horizontal overhangs sag or warp without supports, and powder inside closed cavities cannot be removed. Overhang angles, minimum wall thickness, holes for removing powder and whether supports can be taken off are therefore included as conditions of the optimization. Changing dimensions slightly without changing the topology describes size or shape optimization, and a method that does not constrain the amount of material does not reduce weight.

additive-manufacturing-016.question: In metal binder jetting, a binder is jetted onto each powder layer to form the part (the green part). Which statement about this part is correct?
choices: The powder is melted and solidified by a laser during building, so the as-built part is nearly dense, but rapid cooling leaves large residual stress that must be relieved
The powder is only held together by binder and contains much porosity; it is densified by debinding and sintering, so it is built oversize to allow for large shrinkage
The binder reacts with the metal during sintering to form a hard strengthening phase, so there is almost no shrinkage and the part can be used at its as-built dimensions
additive-manufacturing-016.explanation: Binder jetting does not melt the metal during building. The green part, in which the powder particles are merely joined by binder, keeps the many pores of the packed powder and is weak, so it is densified by debinding, which removes the binder by heating, and by high-temperature sintering. It shrinks a great deal in the process: densifying from 55% relative density, for example, gives a linear shrinkage of about 18% even if isotropic, so the part is built oversize and sagging under its own weight must also be considered. Large residual stress from melting and rapid cooling is characteristic of powder bed fusion, not binder jetting. The binder is meant to be removed in debinding, and residual carbon upsets the composition, so it is not used as a strengthening phase.

additive-manufacturing-017.question: In L-PBF, if the scan speed is too high for the laser power, the melted track may fail to stay continuous and solidify as a row of beads (balling). Which is the main cause?
choices: The long, slender melt pool pinches off into several droplets because surface tension acts to reduce its surface area
A deep vapor depression forms in the melt pool and collapses, and the ejected droplets pile up on the track and solidify
Cooling becomes slower, so coarse dendrites grow in the melt pool and make the surface of the track uneven
additive-manufacturing-017.explanation: At high scan speed the melt pool becomes long and slender. A free liquid cylinder is unstable to necking at wavelengths longer than its circumference (π times its diameter), because breaking up into droplets reduces its surface area (the Plateau–Rayleigh instability). In L-PBF a melt pool longer than about π times its width is used as a rule of thumb for balling, but support from the layer below shifts the actual limit, for example with the penetration depth. The beads that form solidify without wetting the layer below properly, causing surface roughness and lack of fusion. Oxide films on the powder or substrate, which impair wetting, also promote balling. Collapse of a deep vapor depression causes keyhole pores and spatter when the heat input is too large. A faster scan cools faster, so slower cooling is the wrong way round.

additive-manufacturing-018.question: In L-PBF, the direction of the laser scan lines is often rotated by a fixed angle (for example 67°) from one layer to the next, or each layer is divided into small islands scanned in different directions. What is the main purpose?
choices: Rotating the scan direction raises the volumetric energy density of each layer, so lack-of-fusion pores are reduced
Changing the scan direction eliminates the columnar grains that grow along the build direction, so all grains become fine and equiaxed
Residual stress tends to be largest along scan lines, so spreading the directions reduces directional bias in stress and distortion
additive-manufacturing-018.explanation: A melted track is strongly constrained along its length as it cools and contracts, so residual stress tends to be largest along the scan direction, and longer scan lines give larger stress. Shortening the lines by scanning in islands and rotating the direction every layer keeps the stress from lining up in one direction, reducing biased distortion and cracking. Because 67 and 180 have no common factor other than 1, rotating by 67° takes 180 layers to return to the same direction, which also weakens texture. The volumetric energy density P/(v·h·t) is set by power, speed, hatch spacing and layer thickness and does not change with direction. Epitaxial growth from the previous layer continues, so the columnar grains do not turn into equiaxed grains.

additive-manufacturing-019.question: In L-PBF the build plate is lowered by t = 30 µm for each layer before powder is spread. The packing fraction (relative density) of the spread powder is 0.50, and the melted powder shrinks to full density in the thickness direction only. Because the depression left by the shrinkage of the previous layer is also filled by the next powder, the thickness of each spread powder layer approaches a constant value as layers build up. Which is closest to that value?
choices: About 30 µm
About 60 µm
About 15 µm
additive-manufacturing-019.explanation: The part grows by t per layer, so in the steady state the consolidated thickness 0.50T of a spread powder layer of thickness T must equal t. T = t/0.50 = 60 µm. The first layer is 30 µm but shrinks to 15 µm when melted, so the second layer is 30 + 15 = 45 µm, the third about 52.5 µm, and within a few layers the thickness approaches about 60 µm. About 30 µm takes the plate drop itself as the powder thickness, and about 15 µm multiplies by the packing fraction instead of dividing. Because the actual powder layer is thicker than the nominal layer thickness, the laser conditions must be chosen to melt powder of that thickness and fuse it into the layer below.

additive-manufacturing-020.question: Metal L-PBF commonly uses near-spherical powder made by gas atomization. Which is the main reason?
choices: It flows and packs well, so the recoater can spread thin, uniform layers and the powder bed packing density is stable
A sphere has the largest surface area per unit volume and absorbs laser light well, so the powder melts with less energy
Gas-atomized powder contains no oxygen at all, so no oxide inclusions form in the built part
additive-manufacturing-020.explanation: In L-PBF a powder layer a few tens of micrometers thick must be spread evenly for every layer by a blade or roller recoater. In gas atomization a stream of molten metal is broken up by gas jets and the droplets solidify in flight, so surface tension makes the particles nearly spherical; they hardly interlock, flow well and pack without large gaps. The layer thickness and packing density are therefore stable, preventing lack of fusion and nonuniformity. Water-atomized powder is irregular and flows poorly, and suits pressing and sintering. A sphere has the smallest surface area for a given volume, not the largest. Gas-atomized powder also carries a thin surface oxide, and its oxygen content rises with reuse, so it must be controlled.
